articles.title: Rohingya activist says it’s unfair to send refugees back to Myanmar
articles.summary: Rohingya activist says it’s unfair to send refugees back to Myanmar
articles.body:
Rohingya activist says it’s unfair to send refugees back to Myanmar

‘It’s very unfair to send us back to the place we fled from’, says Rohingya rights activist Nur Sadek. Nearly 1,500 Myanmar migrants, including Rohingya refugees, arrived in Myanmar as part of Malaysia’s repatriation push to return 5,000 migrants. The UN and rights groups say it’s unsafe for them to return.

articles.title: Can Yemen retake territory seized by Houthis?
articles.summary: The group has taken control of much of the Red Sea coast.
articles.body:
Yemen’s government has launched an operation to retake territory held by the Houthis and restore its full control of the country.

The Iran-backed Houthi rebel force, also known as Ansar Allah, has made significant territorial gains in the past month, seizing large areas on the Red Sea coast.

In response, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan have met to discuss the situation in Yemen.

In August, they signed a joint defence pact, which is being tested by this conflict.

So, what are the regional dynamics at play?

articles.title: Yemeni military says it has retaken Mokha and 'secured' Red Sea waterway
articles.summary: Saudi-backed forces say they seized the port city of Mocha, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, at the start of an offensive against the Houthis.
articles.body:
Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they have retaken control of the Red Sea port city of Mokha and "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the start of a major offensive against the Iran-backed Houthi movement.

The Yemeni military said National Shield, Giants Brigades and Tihama Resistance forces had captured Mokha on Monday afternoon with the help of Saudi air strikes.

Hours earlier, the military said its forces had seized Dhubab airport, 45km (27 miles) to the south, and were besieging Houthi fighters inside the nearby town.

There was no immediate comment from the Houthis, but Houthi-run media denied that government forces had made advances in Dhubab.

The government said operations had also begun on other fronts on Monday, including the capital Sanaa, which fell to the Houthis at the start of the civil war 12 years ago.

Meanwhile, a Saudi-led military coalition said its fighter jets were providing "round-the-clock" air support to the pro-government forces and had destroyed 324 "high-value" targets since the start of the offensive.

Saudi air strikes killed a schoolgirl and a woman in the Sanhan and Saawan districts of Sanaa on Monday, according to Houth-run Al Masirah TV.

Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdul Salam said Saudi Arabia was committing "dozens of massacres" and that it must "bear all the consequences".

The Houthi-run Humanitarian Operations Co-ordination Centre warned civilian airlines that Saudi airspace, except for the skies above the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina, was no longer safe because it had become "a theatre of operations".

On Sunday, the head of Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council announced the beginning of an offensive, dubbed Operation Yemen Dawn, aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.

Rashad al-Alimi insisted that all opportunities for de-escalation had been exhausted and called on all forces to carry out their assigned missions "until the country is liberated from the grip of the Houthi terrorist militia".

It came after the Houthis reportedly cut a mountain road near the south-western city of Taiz, effectively leaving government forces and residents there surrounded.

The Houthis also said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at oil facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia in retaliation for dozens of Saudi strikes on their territory.

According to BBC Verify, satellite imagery from Saturday shows thick, dark smoke coming from the site of a strike at the Aramco Riyadh Refinery, in the city's south-east.

A similar plume of smoke can be seen rising from the Khurais Central Processing Facility as well as from a potential strike point in satellite imagery from Sunday.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and quickly ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim (Mayyun) Island.

They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

At least 959 people have been killed and 5,000 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry.

The UN says another 197,000 people have been displaced.

articles.title: England's Jordan Pickford 'almost caused crash' with careless driving
articles.summary: The goalkeeper was pulled over by police after ignoring a give way sign, forcing two cars to brake.
articles.body:
England goalkeeper Jordan Pickford nearly caused a crash with two other cars during a bout of careless driving in his £200,000 Lamborghini supercar, a court has heard.

The 32-year-old was pulled over by police after ignoring a give way sign, forcing two cars to slam on the brakes, and then speeding off into the distance.

The incident happened in the Cheshire town of Knutsford on 14 April, sparking a criminal prosecution for driving without due care or attention.

Pickford, who has 336 appearances for Everton and 92 England caps, has pleaded guilty to the charge and will next appear at Chester Magistrates' Court on 7 December.

According to court documents, PC Cecil Ricardo, from Cheshire Police, said he had just left the station when he saw Pickford's blue Lamborghini Urus complete with personalised number plates.

"I was stationary on Bexton Road, Knutsford, waiting for traffic signals to turn green," he wrote.

"I then witnessed a blue Lamborghini Urus driving along Princess Street.

"It reached the junction with Toft Road, completely ignored the give way lines and pulled onto Toft Road causing two vehicles to slam on their brakes to avoid a collision.

"The Lamborghini then sped down Toft Road, Knutsford."

Ricardo said he activated his lights and siren to set off in pursuit of the Lamborghini, noticing he was driving at 50mph (80.4 kmh) while the Lamborghini "was still pulling away".

"The speed limit on that stretch of Toft Road, Knutsford, is 30mph," he noted.

The officer said Pickford appeared to notice the chasing police car and pulled over.

Pickford pleaded guilty in writing and told Warrington Magistrates Court: "I would like to attend court to put forward my mitigation."

His case was formally adjourned last week.

Pickford, who started his career at Sunderland before loan spells at six clubs including Burton Albion, Bradford City and Preston North End, has featured for England at the 2018, 2022 and 2026 World Cups, and was in goal for the country's Euro 2020 and 2024 final appearances.

articles.title: Latest US military strike on alleged drug boat kills four in Caribbean
articles.summary: UN warns US boat strikes in the Caribbean counter-drug war may violate international law and human rights principles.
articles.body:
The United States has conducted another strike on an alleged drug trafficking boat in the Caribbean, killing four, according to the US military.

US Southern Command said late Sunday that it struck alleged drug traffickers operating along “established narco-trafficking routes” in the eastern Pacific and Caribbean, following its standard reporting pattern for military operations of suspected cartels across the multinational maritime zones.

The latest attack brings the death toll from US military boat strikes to at least 235 deaths across 70 attacks, since the administration of US President Donald Trump first launched its counter-narcoterrorism campaign , termed Operation Southern Spear, in September of last year.

At the time, Trump characterised the fight against cartels in Latin America as an active “armed conflict” while defending the strikes as a necessary escalation to curb illicit drug trafficking and reduce fatal US overdoses.

The move comes as United Nations experts warn that the strikes violate international law and could amount to crimes against humanity.

Despite releasing footage on X showing the explosion that destroyed the moving vessel, the US military has offered no evidence that the targeted boat was ferrying drugs.

The Trump administration has been actively seeking regional security agreements across Latin America to expand joint military operations against what it has designated as criminal cartels. The deals come under the US-led Shield of the Americas coalition , launched in March. The president has pledged the undertaking will use “unmatched military might” to dismantle drug cartels while simultaneously countering Chinese economic influence in the Western Hemisphere.

During a visit to Panama in August, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that Colombia, Guatemala and Honduras had agreed to joint counter-crime military operations on their soil, a statement Guatemala quickly disputed to clarify its sovereignty and boundaries within the 19-member alliance.

articles.title: Would the Conservatives' plan make new houses £50,000 cheaper?
articles.summary: BBC Verify looks into the shadow chancellor's plan to cut some building regulations to reduce construction costs.
articles.body:
Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith has said his party, if it was returned to power, would take £50,000 off the cost of building a new home in England and Wales by cutting back on regulations.

The £50,000 figure claimed by Griffith reflects estimates by the housebuilding industry of the costs of new regulations and taxes.

However, construction and housing experts warn that some of the savings could ultimately lead to higher government spending on schools, roads, and affordable housing.

And some analysts also warn the Conservative plans to scrap environmental regulations could potentially push up household energy bills in future.

Where does the £50,000 figure come from?

The Conservatives argue a number of regulations are adding to the cost of constructing and delivering new private homes.

The Community Infrastructure Levy - a charge on certain new developments in England and Wales which councils can use to fund local infrastructure such as roads, schools and play areas

The Future Homes Standard which requires new-build homes in England to meet higher energy-efficiency standards and use low-carbon heating such as heat pumps rather than gas boilers

Section 106 which can require developers to provide a proportion of social or affordable housing in England as part of a new development.

The Tories say they will scrap or reform these and other regulations, saying: "All in all, we will cut the cost of delivering and therefore buying a new home by up to £50,000."

BBC Verify has asked the Conservatives for a full breakdown of their figure.

What does the construction industry say?

The Home Builders Federation (HBF) has estimated that new regulations, taxes and inflation - since 2020 - have increased the cost of building an individual new home in England and Wales by £76,000.

It says this represents around 20% of the value of an average new home.

£10,200 comes from the Future Homes Standard

£12,700 in environmental protection measures such as "nutrient neutrality" and "biodiversity net gain"

Excluding a £37,000 increase in the costs of material and labour, the HBF estimates that regulations and taxes have added around £42,000 to the cost of building a new home.

The Conservatives' estimate is slightly higher than the HBF's figure. The HBF also includes nearly £8,000 to reflect changes in building regulations. The Conservatives have not said they would find savings by scrapping all of those.

The party's plan also assumes the savings they have highlighted would be passed on to buyers rather than raising house builders' profits.

Noble Francis of trade body the Construction Products Association (CPA) told BBC Verify that new costs imposed on builders through regulations and taxes in recent years - including the time firms spend navigating the regulatory system - are a serious constraint on residential construction rates.

The Labour government is well off track in terms of meeting its target of building 1.5 million net additional dwellings in England over the course of this parliament - which requires an annual building rate of around 300,000 homes per year.

In the year to June only around 203,000 were built, according to official estimates.

However, Francis also said: "It's easy for any party not in government to just claim they will get rid of red tape and cut costs but both the Conservatives and Labour have been in power in the last five years and have added extra costs to house building."

The Future Homes Standard, for instance, was first proposed in 2019 when Conservative Prime Minister Boris Johnson was in power.

Other analysts point out that the upfront construction cost savings from the plan could potentially lead to higher government spending in the future.

Housing expert Anna Clarke said: "Cutting the costs of house building by £50,000 would be really helpful in getting much-needed new homes built.

"But if you don't get developers to pay for new schools and infrastructure you need to pay for them some other way."

And some analysts argue that updated environmental building standards, such as requiring heat pumps rather than gas boilers in new homes, are forecast to save households money in the long-term by reducing their domestic energy bills.

Dr Richard Lowes of clean energy advocates the Regulatory Assistance Project told BBC Verify: "If the energy bill implications are not carefully considered, households may be lumbered with very high bills for decades.

"The lowest running costs can typically be achieved with heat pumps paired with solar and batteries."

Additional reporting by Nicholas Barrett and Daniel Wainwright

articles.title: Indian man on a spouse visa convicted of money laundering in Austin, worked as a coordinator for India-based call center scammers
articles.summary: Bhavesh Kumar Thakkar, a 45-year-old Indian man, has been convicted of two counts related to wire fraud and money laundering in Texas.
articles.body: Bhavesh Kumar Thakkar, a 45-year-old Indian man, has been convicted of two counts related to wire fraud and money laundering in Texas. According to court documents, Thakkar was part of an elaborate fraud scheme that went on from September 2022 to 2025 -- with Rakesh Barot, Dhruv Rajeshbhai Mangukiya and Kishan Rajeshkumar Patel. All of them were part of the senior scam across the country, where senior citizens are told to get gold using all their savings. They are then convinced to hand over the gold to their courier partners claiming that they are federal officers who will protest their gold.In his role, Thakkar, who is on a spouse visa, served as a US-based coordinator for the receipt and laundering of fraud proceeds in the form of cash and gold obtained from elderly victims across the country. The fraud proceeds were obtained by call center scammers based in India. He also personally received some of those funds from couriers such as Mangukiya and Patel. The funds were shipped to Los Angeles and New York before being laundered overseas. Thakkar was directly connected to over $150 million in fraud proceeds scammed from elderly victims across the United States.“Foreign actors, both abroad and here in the United States, cannot be allowed to target Americans, especially our most vulnerable citizens,” said US Attorney Simmons. “Many victims lose a significant portion of their life savings to these scammers, leaving victims vulnerable and hopeless. When we find them, we will do all we can to take from them the same sense of freedom and comfort they stole from their victims.”“Protecting our elderly citizens from those who would defraud them out of their hard-earned money is a high priority for the FBI,” said FBI San Antonio Division Special Agent in Charge Daniel Faith. “This defendant was found guilty of working with others to scam a large number of vulnerable senior citizens out of millions of dollars. We’re grateful to all of our partners in this case, including numerous FBI Field Offices, Indian authorities via our Legat New Delhi and the Granite Shoals Police Department.”In 2025, Mangukiya and Patel were sentenced to 97 months and 63 months in federal prison, respectively. Barot pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit money laundering and is awaiting sentencing.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Mystery death at Russian plague lab triggers sweeping precautions as US watches closely
articles.summary: Darya Shipilova's death at a Siberian plague research institute triggered quarantines and mass observation, but Russia has not confirmed what killed her.
articles.body: Russian authorities have quarantined a hospital and placed scores of people under medical observation after a 28-year-old employee at a Siberian plague research institute died from a mysterious case of pneumonia, fueling fears — still unconfirmed — that she may have contracted pneumonic plague. Darya Shipilova worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East. Russian health authorities say extensive testing found no evidence that her illness was caused by pathogens linked to her work, but officials have yet to publicly identify what killed her. The extraordinary precautions surrounding the case have fueled speculation inside and outside Russia. Reuters reported Oct. 5 that all known contacts had been traced and placed under medical supervision and that authorities said no new cases had been identified among employees of the institute. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that the U.S. was "watching and monitoring it closely," adding, "I don’t think it’s cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause just to keep an eye on it." US MONITORING SUSPECTED FATAL PNEUMONIC PLAGUE CASE IN RUSSIA, STATE DEPARTMENT OFFICIAL SAYS Rubio said information released by Russia appeared to show "there was a worker at the lab that was infected" and concern that the illness could have spread internally. He noted that travel between Russia and the U.S. is limited but warned that "something like that gets out, it just quickly spreads." The comments follow a State Department statement to Fox News on Oct. 4 that Washington was monitoring the case alongside the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and other federal agencies. The official stressed that many details remained unconfirmed and urged Moscow to provide accurate information quickly. Additional reporting provided Monday by East2West news agency said more than 60 employees remained confined inside the Irkutsk institute and nearly 200 people who had contact with Shipilova had been placed under observation. Those precise figures have not been officially confirmed. The agency also reported that neighboring countries, including Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan, had increased border health precautions following the case. The hospital in Shelekhov, just outside Irkutsk, where Shipilova was treated, has been placed under quarantine and temporarily stopped admitting or discharging patients, according to The Associated Press. Irkutsk Gov. Igor Kobzev described the case as a suspected "particularly dangerous infection." SCIENTISTS CRACK THE CODE ON NEW VACCINE FOR DEADLY PLAGUE BACTERIA Adding to the unusual response, Anna Popova, the head of Russia’s public health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Irkutsk for an emergency meeting after Shipilova’s death, Reuters reported. A nearby aluminum plant also ordered employees to wear masks as a precaution. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov urged the public to rely on official information rather than "rumors or speculation." Rospotrebnadzor said Sunday that Shipilova was diagnosed with "pneumonia of unknown etiology" and that testing detected "no microorganisms associated with the patient’s professional activities." The agency also said an investigation found no laboratory incident involving pathogenic microorganisms. Pneumonic plague is a severe form of plague caused by Yersinia pestis that can spread from person to person through respiratory droplets during close contact. It can be successfully treated with antibiotics when treatment begins early. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Russian officials continue to insist there is no evidence of a plague outbreak and say the epidemiological situation remains stable. For now, however, the central question remains unanswered: what caused Shipilova’s fatal pneumonia — and why authorities imposed such extensive containment measures if no dangerous pathogen has been detected.

articles.title: Jeremy Clarkson makes surprise appearance at Tory conference
articles.summary: The former Top Gear presenter and star of Clarkson's Farm also said farmers were being "attacked" from every angle.
articles.body:
Jeremy Clarkson has said it had been a "terrible" year for farming due to the hot weather, at a surprise appearance at the Conservative Party conference in Birmingham.

The former Top Gear presenter and star of Clarkson's Farm also said farmers were being "attacked" from every angle by rising costs, but he was optimistic about the future.

He was greeted by loud applause from the Tory faithful, but joked that "a lot of people have come dressed as seats, I notice, around the edges there".

In a question and answer session alongside land agent Charlie Ireland, he also criticised the economic conditions faced by business owners, asking: "Why would anybody set up a business in this country right now?"

Clarkson - who also hosts ITV's Who Wants to be a Millionaire - was introduced to the stage by the Conservative shadow environment secretary Victoria Atkins.

Asked what kind of year he had had on the farm, Clarkson said: "We worked really hard all year and we ended up with, I think I'm right in saying, three ounces of hen food.

"It was an absolute disaster on the farming side but, I mean, luckily we've got other projects going on now.

"But the farming is very, very difficult – very, very difficult at the moment."

He added: "I'm very fortunate that I do have other income streams and newspaper columns, but if you're an ordinary farmer, it's not just the weather.

"Remember, it's as Charlie was saying, the attacks come from everywhere – whether it's Iran or Ukraine or taxes or energy costs – whatever it might be, it's just relentless."

The TV presenter has long been a Conservative supporter and was involved in the campaign against the Labour government's inheritance tax plans for farmers .

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government would levy inheritance tax on family farms in the party's first budget.

But the plan was watered down last year following the farmers' campaign and pressure from some of Labour's rural MPs.

Responding to Clarkson's comments, a government source said: "We are working with farmers to strengthen domestic food production and make supply chains more resilient as we build a stronger and more profitable farming sector together."

Clarkson also joked about comments by Labour MP Jenny Riddell-Carpenter who said the Britain of country pubs and black Labradors was a "nostalgic" false memory.

He joked that he was a "socialist" because he drinks lager and has two fox red Labradors, after it was reported Riddell-Carpenter told a Labour conference fringe event she feared the far right deciding what the vision of rural areas is.

Riddell-Carpenter had said: "It'll be that warm ale, a black Labrador by your feet in a pub that doesn't exist, and with symbolism of fox hunting all around them. It'll be a very far-right nostalgic vision of Britain that we don't want to have, (that) never really existed."

articles.title: Yemeni gov’t forces aim for Sanaa, but Houthi defeat will be a challenge
articles.summary: Yemeni government forces claim strategic advances near Bab al-Mandeb strait amid a major anti-Houthi offensive.
articles.body:
Yemeni government forces have claimed advances along the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait after the head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, ⁠Rashad al-Alimi, announced the start of a major offensive to capture all territories lost to the Houthis.

On Monday, forces aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognised government claimed the advance and headed north along the Red Sea coast, and said they had retaken the town of Dhubab and port city of Mocha. They also earlier said that they had launched a “strategic offensive” on the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.

Government forces are also attempting to reverse gains made by the Houthis in recent days around the key city of Taiz, in southwestern Yemen.

The Houthis, an Iranian-allied movement, have held the capital Sanaa since September 2014, before making other territorial gains in northern and western Yemen.

After four years of relative calm, fighting flared once again in July, before a Houthi offensive in early September saw the group make sweeping gains along the Red Sea coast, including the port city of Mocha and Bab al-Mandeb.

The Yemeni government, backed by Saudi Arabia, is now attempting to regain that lost territory, but still faces divisions within the anti-Houthi camp.

“The [internationally recognised government’s] ground forces are big on paper and quite sizeable, but scattered across a bunch of fronts and running on old pre-war gear, so they can hold their lines but [currently] can’t push the Houthis out of their mountain strongholds,” Raiman al-Hamdani, a London-based Yemen analyst, told Al Jazeera.

The most recent fighting hints at a new escalation in the conflict, al-Hamdani said.

“This all seems to be moving into a more dangerous phase, and while the appetite for a full-scale war may exist among elements of the leadership on both sides, the reality is more complicated,” al-Hamdani said.

“In the longer term, the more plausible outcome is not the military destruction of one side by the other, but a negotiated and imperfect political settlement in which the Houthis retain substantial influence in northern Yemen, Saudi Arabia obtains greater security guarantees, and Yemen’s competing political and military factions are forced into some form of power-sharing arrangement,” al-Hamdani added.

“The problem is that reaching that point may require another period of serious escalation before any settlement.”

Ahmed al-Shalafi, Al Jazeera’s Yemen correspondent and a specialist in Yemeni affairs, reported that the recent moves by the Yemeni government show “complete operational and political integration”.

“These moves lend a serious and decisive dimension to the announced battle to liberate Sanaa and restore the state,” he said.

Al-Shalafi said the government’s offensive is intended to start the confrontation on their own terms, rather than allowing the Houthis to dictate the stages of the war.

And even if the United States and Iran agree a deal to end their ongoing conflict, which began in late February, it might not seriously impact the fighting in Yemen.

Nicholas Brumfield, an independent Yemen analyst, told Al Jazeera that he believes the balance of power has not yet shifted in favour of either side.

“The Houthis are going to keep pushing in Taiz and Marib,” he said. “[Government] forces have been better on the defensive in Taiz … But the Houthis have been able to push in all directions at once in a way [government] forces just aren’t.”

However, Saeed Thabet, the head of Al Jazeera’s Yemen bureau, said the government’s advances, coming soon after al-Alimi’s announcement of the beginning of a new large-scale offensive against the Houthis, were a way of demonstrating that the government was serious about reversing Houthi gains.

“The military expansion is a message that the government is determined to implement what it says in its statements,” Thabet said. “In the past, a lot of Yemenis would not take these statements seriously.”

“The government forces will now attempt to … control Taiz’s Red Sea coast,” he added. “It will also attempt to contain the Houthi infiltration into some villages and areas in Taiz governorate, especially in al-Shamayatayn and al-Waziya districts. Sources there have told us that government security forces are sweeping those areas and capturing some [Houthi] armed men.”

articles.title: In 2023, recycled turbine-blade fibre in asphalt raised laboratory low-temperature ultimate strain by 34.2%, indicating greater deformation tolerance before cracking
articles.summary: A 2023 study reveals that integrating recycled wind turbine blade fibre into asphalt can improve its low-temperature crack tolerance by 34.2%, making roadways more durable and sustainable.
articles.body: Recycled wind turbine blade material could improve the ability of asphalt mixtures to withstand deformation at low temperatures, according to a 2023 laboratory study. Researchers found that combining recycled wind turbine blade (rWTB) powder and fibre led to an increase of the asphalt mixture’s ultimate strain by 34.2%,indicating that the modified mixture could tolerate greater deformation before cracking.The study published in Frontiers in Materials by Tianhui Lan, Bingze Wang, Junchao Zhang, Hao Wei and Xu Liu, investigated whether waste from retired wind turbine blades could be incorporated into asphalt mixtures. The material of the recycled blade was tested with a powder smaller than 0.075 millimetres and fibre ranging from 0.075 to 9.5 millimetres. According to the paper, the work addressed two materials challenges at once: the 20-25 years lifespan of wind turbine blades, and the fact that most blade materials are made of glass-fibre-reinforced plastics. The recovery and reuse of these blade materials were difficult because they contained 60%–70% fibre and 30%–40% cross-linked thermoset polymer. This led researchers to examine mechanical recycling, which produces blade material in forms that can be reused in other products. In the asphalt tests, rWTB powder replaced portions of the fine filler at concentrations of 5%, 10%, and 15%. Concurrently, rWTB fibre replaced part of the fine aggregate at concentrations of 0.1%, 0.2%, and 0.3%The recycled fibre changed how asphalt responded to low temperatures Researchers evaluated the modified asphalt mixtures for rutting resistance at 60°C using wheel tracking tests. Using three-point bending tests low-temperature cracking resistance at −10°C was tested and water stability using Marshall immersion tests. The addition of rWTB powder alone yielded an increase of about 10% in ultimate strain when compared to the reference mixture, and when recycled fibre was introduced, the effect became more pronounced. At the highest fibre concentration of 0.3%, ultimate strain increased by 28.2% compared to the reference mixture, while a blend of 0.3% rWTB fibre and 10% recycled powder achieved a 34.2% increase.This improvement was attributed to the physical role of the recycled fibre within the asphalt mortar, microscopic examination showed that the fibre was wrapped by asphalt mortar, with a tight interface between the two materials. This allowed the fibre to transfer loads and distribute stress through a bridging effect and the mixture to accommodate greater deformation under low-temperature conditions. Moreover, the powder and fibre also produced different effects. Moreover, the powder and fibre also produced different effects. At low temperatures, recycled powder improved flexural strength, while the fibre mainly increased ultimate strain.Powder and fibre worked at different scales, with trade-offs The researchers found that using the two recycled blade forms together could modify the asphalt mixture at different scales. The powder interacted with the asphalt mortar, while the larger fibres provided reinforcement within the mixture. Thermogravimetric testing also indicated that the recycled blade material had high thermal stability below 200°C, a range relevant to asphalt mixture compaction, paving and service, while significant mass loss occurred at around 350°C and 600°C.However, the study didn’t establish that every increase in recycled fibre yielded an improvement across all properties because fibre could potentially reduce flexural strength and water stability, when different sizes of fibres were unevenly distributed and could form rod-like stacks. This meant that when designing the asphalt mixture, both the fibre content and particle-size range needed to be considered.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: What Fox News CEO said on Karoline Leavitt joining the channel as a contributor from November 1
articles.summary: Fox News Media CEO Suzanne Scott said former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt has a distinct understanding of today's political landscape --
articles.body: Fox News Media CEO Suzanne Scott said former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt has a distinct understanding of today's political landscape -- as Leavitt finalizes her next career move as a contributor to the channel in less than two months after she left the Trump administration.Leavitt, 29, will begin her new role on November 1 and provide commentary and analysis across Fox News' programming, including its news and opinion platforms."Karoline's firsthand experience in the White House and on the presidential campaign trail gives her a distinct understanding of today's political landscape," Fox News Media CEO Suzanne Scott said in announcing the appointment.Leavitt said she was grateful for the opportunity to become an official member of the Fox News Media team."I look forward to bringing my unique perspective from my experience as White House Press Secretary, along with the same energy and candor that defined my tenure, to Fox's millions of viewers across their many platforms," she said.Leavitt served as President Donald Trump's press secretary from January 2025 until August 2026. She became the youngest person in US history to hold the position. Before joining the White House, she worked on Trump's 2024 presidential campaign and served as a spokesperson for MAGA Inc.Why did Karoline Leavitt leave the White House?Leavitt announced her departure in August, saying she had made a "bittersweet decision" after concluding that the demanding press secretary role made it difficult for her to spend enough time with her two young children.She had returned to the White House after maternity leave following the birth of her second child.President Trump, while announcing her departure, said he understood and respected her decision to spend more time with her family. He also indicated that Leavitt would remain an outside adviser.Leavitt subsequently moved back to New Hampshire with her family. Reports at the time also said she planned to remain involved in supporting Trump and the Republican Party.Karoline Leavitt's Fox News connectionLeavitt's move to Fox News is not entirely new territory for her. She interned at Fox News during the 2016 presidential election before beginning her political career.She is also the second former Trump press secretary to join Fox News. Kayleigh McEnany, who served as Trump's press secretary during his first administration, later became a Fox News host and contributor.Leavitt's appointment continues a long-standing pattern of former White House press secretaries moving into television roles after leaving government.She will join Fox News at a time when the network continues to feature former political officials and campaign figures across its news and opinion programming.Who is the new White House press secretary?Trump has not yet announced a permanent successor to Leavitt as White House press secretary.Leavitt served as the administration's chief spokesperson for more than a year and regularly appeared at White House briefings to defend the president's policies and respond to questions from reporters.After leaving her role, she left Washington and moved to New Hampshire, where she grew up.You use AI every day. articles.title: British Airways flight to Chicago drops 28,000 feet, returns to London
articles.summary: A British Airways passenger jet declared an emergency and descended rapidly while flying from London to Chicago.
articles.body: LONDON — A British Airways passenger jet flying from London to Chicago descended 28,000 feet in just seven minutes after declaring an emergency due to an unspecified “technical issue,” the airline said Monday. The Boeing 777 took off at 12:15 p.m. local time (7:15 a.m. ET) but started descending just 30 minutes later while flying over Ireland, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware. The plane turned around and spent around four hours zigzagging over the Bristol Channel, a waterway to the west of England, before landing back at London Heathrow Airport at 5 p.m. local time (noon ET). “The aircraft landed safely after our highly-trained pilots returned to Heathrow following a technical issue,” British Airways said in an emailed statement. “Customers disembarked the aircraft normally and our teams are working to get their travel plans back on track as quickly as possible.” Heathrow did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Passengers will likely be put up in hotels by the airline until another flight can be arranged, as stipulated by the U.K. Civil Aviation Authority. Britain’s National Air Traffic Service (NATS) came under scrutiny last month after two technical problems in the space of two weeks caused major delays at several U.K. airports and hundreds of flights were canceled. NATS blamed software issues for the delays. Britain’s Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander acknowledged the situation had been “deeply frustrating” for passengers. With 84.5 million passengers last year, Heathrow ranked seventh in the table of the world’s busiest airports, according to data published by Airports Council International. Travel from Heathrow was severely disrupted in March last year when a massive fire at an electricity substation caused a predawn power outage at the global transport hub. The closure affected more than 1,300 flights and 200,000 passengers. After investigating 600 items of evidence related to the substation, the National Energy System Operator ruled out suspicious activity in a report saying a preventable moisture fault caused the fire, leaving almost 70,000 homes without power.

articles.title: In 2006, Minnesota rebuilt a street with old pavement strengthened by 10% coal fly ash; after a freeze-thaw cycle, testing found no loss of stiffness
articles.summary: In a groundbreaking study, Minnesota engineers demonstrated the effective use of 10% coal fly ash to strengthen recycled pavement, revealing promising results in durability and performance after freeze-thaw cycles. This method not only enhances road resilience but also promotes sustainability by reusing existing materials.
articles.body: It's not always necessary to remove all that already exists to rebuild a road. Engineers in Waseca, Minnesota, experimented with a more circular strategy: they ground up the old pavement, strengthened the recycled material with coal fly ash, and then replaced it with a fresh asphalt covering. As part of a Minnesota study investigating whether fly ash could stabilise recycled pavement material sufficiently to function as a new road basis, the experiment was conducted on 7th Street and 7th Avenue. Particularly after the restored area experienced its first Minnesota winter, the outcomes were positive.Researchers found that the stabilised layer was stiffer and stronger than the untreated recycled pavement material. Field observations post-freeze-thaw cycle likewise showed no degradation of its modulus, and the researchers noted that they needed a longer period of monitoring.What was done on 7th Street and 7th AvenueThis process is called full-depth reclamation. Instead of ripping out the old asphalt and replacing it with a new aggregate foundation, a road reclaimer pulverised the previous pavement and base material to a depth of approximately 300 millimetres, creating what researchers refer to as recycled pavement material, or RPM.Crews added Class C fly ash to the recycled material at 10% of the dry weight during construction in 2004, according to the University of Wisconsin-Madison project report. During mixing, water was added; the material was compacted one to two hours after mixing, and the stabilised layer was cured for seven days before a fresh hot-mix asphalt surface was placed.Self-cementing Class C fly ash is characterised by a chemical composition that enables it to react with water and generate cementitious products. Therefore, the recovered pavement material has a significantly stronger, stiffer structure than the untreated material alone.How the researchers tested itThe researchers didn’t just rely on one assessment of the pavement. In the field, a soil stiffness gauge and a dynamic cone penetrometer were used, while in the laboratory, tests for resilient modulus, California bearing ratio and unconfined compressive strength were conducted. The case study found that adding fly ash substantially improved the bearing resistance and stiffness of the recycled pavement material. After seven days of curing, laboratory-prepared stabilized material had a resilient modulus of 78 to 119 MPa, compared with roughly 46 to 50 MPa for untreated recycled pavement material.The key test was made after construction. Researchers employed a falling-weight deflectometer to evaluate the stiffness of the underlying layers by applying a controlled load to the pavement and measuring the subsequent deflection. Measurements at Waseca in August 2005, about one year after construction, indicated no degradation in the modulus of the stabilized recycled pavement material after it had been exposed to a winter freeze-thaw cycle. The two sets of field measurements exhibited mean moduli of roughly 262 and 252 MPa, respectively, and statistical testing showed no significant difference between them.This was important since pavement bases are particularly susceptible to damage from freeze-thaw action. If water gets into the substance, it can freeze and expand and then weaken the layer when the temperature rises again. A stabilised base that remains rigid after winter has a significant advantage over a weaker, untreated layer.The numbers that make the narrative complicatedThe Waseca field result should not be interpreted as indicative of the fact that fly ash-stabilized pavement is immune to any freeze-thaw exposure. In the larger Minnesota investigation, the stabilised materials were subjected to numerous laboratory freeze-thaw cycles and response was found to be dependent on the base material.The resilient modulus of fly ash-stabilized road-surface gravel dropped by approximately 17% after five laboratory cycles, while the recycled pavement materials examined saw reductions from about 25% to 42%, according to the University of Wisconsin-Madison and Minnesota transportation study report. In a larger collection of stabilised materials, reductions after 12 cycles were no greater than 50%. The gap between the field and laboratory data is significant. In Waseca, pavement field stiffness did not change after one winter, while lab specimens subjected to repeated, controlled freeze-thaw cycles had noticeable losses. The researchers suggested continuing monitoring in the field rather than using the first winter as evidence of permanent durability. Testing has its limits as well. “There were no established criteria specifically for resilient-modulus testing for fly ash-stabilized materials,” the paper said. Taking undisturbed samples from a stabilised pavement could damage the samples and affect the results.The environmental questionAt the Waseca site, drainage was captured in a lysimeter placed under the roadway, allowing the researchers to analyse the chemical composition of the drainage. The assessment found that the detected trace elements remained below US Environmental Protection Agency maximum contaminant levels; manganese, however, exceeded the Minnesota health-risk level cited in the report. “Longer-term monitoring will be needed to understand leaching over the complete service life of the pavement,” the researchers added. That finding qualifies the engineering achievements in an important sense. The use of an industrial by-product can reduce the demand for fresh aggregate. However, the material still needs to be examined for both uniformity and environmental behaviour.What does that meanThe Waseca experiment demonstrated that an old pavement can be part of its replacement. The engineers broke up the existing road, added 10% Class C fly ash and compacted the mixture into a new base. The stabilized layer had substantially greater stiffness and strength than the untreated recycled material. The first winter looked promising: field deflection tests showed no significant change in pavement modulus after freeze-thaw exposure. Laboratory tests, however, showed that repeated freeze-thaw cycles could reduce stiffness in some stabilized materials, while environmental monitoring identified manganese as a separate issue requiring attention.The practical lesson is narrower: the results suggest that fly ash stabilization can strengthen recycled pavement material under the conditions tested. Fly ash stabilisation can be an effective base for recycled pavement and reduce the need to remove existing road material under the conditions evaluated, the results suggest. Rather than assuming the method would perform identically elsewhere, the researchers measured the material, monitored the pavement through winter and examined the drainage.You use AI every day. articles.title: More Than 122,000 Cases of Gatorade Recalled Across the Country: What to Know
articles.summary: More than 122,000 cases of Gatorade have been recalled in 37 states for undeclared food dyes, according to a notice by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA).
articles.body: More than 122,000 cases of Gatorade have been recalled, according to a notice by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). The recall, which was initiated Sept. 25, involves a total of 122,021 cases of 28-ounce bottles of Gatorade Lemon Lime, Gatorade Lemon Lime Zero, Gatorade Orange and Gatorade Orange Zero. The items have been recalled for containing undeclared Yellow No. 6 and/or Yellow No. 5. The affected cases feature the following codes: Lot 091026 DL — June 7, 2027Lot 091126 DL — June 8, 2027Lot 072226 DT — April 18, 2027Lot 072426 TL — April 20, 2027Lot 073126 TL — April 27, 2027Lot 072926 TL — April 25, 2027Lot 073026 TL — April 25, 2027Lot 081026 TL — May 7, 2027Lot 082126 OA — April 18, 2027Lot 080126 DL — April 28, 2027Lot 082026 DL — May 17, 2027Lot 083126 DT — June 7, 2027Lot 082526 KM — May 22, 2027Lot 090426 KM — June 1, 2027Lot 072726 TL — April 23, 2027 The recall affects products distributed in 37 states, including Alabama, Alaska, Arkansas, Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Iowa, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Mississippi, North Carolina, North Dakota, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, Nevada, New York, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Washington and Wisconsin. TODAY.com has reached out to PepsiCo, which owns Gatorade, for comment, but had not heard back by publication. The FDA calls this matter a Class II recall, which is defined as “a situation in which use of or exposure to a violative product may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences or where the probability of serious adverse health consequences is remote.”

articles.title: What is Pneumonic Plague? 200 people under watch as Russia scare puts spotlight on deadly lung infection
articles.summary: Around 200 employees at a Russian anti-plague institute are being monitored after coming into contact with a 27-year-old woman who died following severe
articles.body: Around 200 employees at a Russian anti-plague institute are being monitored after coming into contact with a 27-year-old woman who died following severe pneumonia, amid reports that she may have contracted pneumonic plague.The incident in Irkutsk, a city in eastern Siberia, has raised concerns about a possible outbreak. However, Russian health authorities have said extensive testing has so far found no evidence that the woman was infected with plague or any other microorganism linked to her professional activities.What happened in IrkutskThe woman, an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, was admitted to hospital on September 29 with symptoms of severe pneumonia and was placed on a ventilator.She died overnight between October 1 and 2.On October 2, The Moscow Times reported that an emergency meeting of the Sanitary and Anti-Epidemic Commission was held jointly by Irkutsk region governor Igor Kobzev and Anna Popova, head of Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's national public health and consumer rights agency.“All identified contacts have been placed under medical observation. Currently, they show no signs of illness, and laboratory tests are negative,” Kobzev said.He added that Rospotrebnadzor was implementing “a full range of anti-epidemic measures”.Local media reported two theories about how the woman could have been exposed to the bacterium.One theory was that she had recently returned from a work trip to the Buryatia region, where a plague outbreak was reportedly being reported near the border with Mongolia.Another suggested that she may have accidentally broken a test tube containing a dangerous bacterium in a laboratory.These reports led to speculation that she had contracted pneumonic plague. But on Sunday, Rospotrebnadzor said she had been diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology”. It said “extensive” testing had found “no microorganisms associated with the patient’s professional activities”.What is pneumonic plaguePlague is a serious infectious disease caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium that normally circulates among small mammals and their fleas but can infect humans.It is a zoonotic disease, meaning it can spread between animals and humans. Plague has three main forms: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.Pneumonic plague is the most serious form because it infects the lungs and can progress extremely rapidly. Unlike bubonic plague, which primarily affects the lymph nodes, pneumonic plague can also spread directly from person to person through respiratory droplets.According to Dr Vikas Mittal, Director and Pulmonologist at CK Birla Hospital in Delhi, pneumonic plague presents as a rapidly progressive form of pneumonia, typically causing fever, chest pain, cough and breathlessness.The infection can develop in two ways.Primary pneumonic plague occurs when a person inhales respiratory secretions or aerosolised droplets from an infected animal or person. It can also occur following laboratory exposure.Secondary pneumonic plague develops when the bacteria spread through the bloodstream in someone who already has bubonic or septicemic plague. This can happen when treatment is delayed.What happens when someone gets pneumonic plagueThe illness usually begins abruptly and can worsen very quickly.“Illness is typically abrupt, with sudden onset of dyspnea, high fever, pleuritic chest pain, and cough that may be accompanied by characteristic bloody sputum,” Dr Mittal said.The disease can initially resemble other severe forms of pneumonia, making early recognition important.Chest imaging also does not provide a definitive diagnosis. “Chest imaging is not specific and may show bronchopneumonia, consolidation, cavities, or pleural effusions; hilar or mediastinal adenopathy can sometimes be seen,” Dr Mittal said.The speed at which treatment begins is critical.“Pneumonic plague can be rapidly fatal unless effective antibiotics are started early, and untreated mortality is very high,” Dr Mittal said, adding that delays in starting antibiotics are associated with a higher risk of death.How does pneumonic plague spreadPrimary pneumonic plague can occur after inhalation exposure to respiratory droplets from an infected person or animal.The incubation period is short, ranging from a few hours to a few days. Human-to-human transmission through respiratory droplets has been documented, but Dr Mittal said it appears most likely to occur after very close contact.This means a suspected case can have significant public health implications, particularly if the illness is not recognised quickly.However, outbreaks can be contained. Treating infected patients promptly and providing preventive treatment to people who have been exposed are key measures used to stop transmission.How is pneumonic plague diagnosedBecause the early symptoms can resemble severe pneumonia caused by many other infections, doctors need a high degree of suspicion when there is a relevant exposure history.Diagnosis can be established by isolating Yersinia pestis through culture, or through appropriate serological or rapid testing.“Timely diagnosis requires a high index of suspicion,” Dr Mittal said.Because of the possibility of respiratory transmission, infection-control measures are also important.“Patients suspected of having plague should be placed on droplet precautions until pneumonia has been ruled out, sputum cultures are negative, and at least 48 hours of effective antimicrobial therapy has been administered,” Dr Mittal said.Countries raise alertThe reports from Irkutsk have also prompted countries to increase precautionary measures, according to The Moscow Times.Kazakhstan's health ministry said sanitary and quarantine checks were being carried out at state border crossings. So far, it said, no arrivals had been found to have elevated temperatures, signs of illness or suspected particularly dangerous infections.In Kyrgyzstan, sanitary and quarantine checkpoints were placed on high alert, with specialists screening people, vehicles and cargo crossing the border.Uzbekistan's sanitary and epidemiological committee also increased the readiness of services responsible for preventing the entry of particularly dangerous infections.On Monday, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said he doesn’t think there is cause for alarm, but the US is watching the case closely, aware that “it could spread quickly” despite the quarantine and other public health protocols.Indian health authorities are actively tracing contacts, with experts claiming there is no cause for public panic or immediate threat to the country.Kremlin urges Russians to ignore rumoursAmid growing speculation online, Kremlin press secretary Dmitry Peskov on Monday urged Russians not to believe rumours about a possible plague outbreak in Irkutsk.“The lead agency with jurisdiction in this area is Rospotrebnadzor. And we should rely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements, without listening to various rumours and speculation,” he said.Additionally, governor Kobzev said no new cases of staff from the Anti-Plague Institute seeking medical attention were identified.For now, Russian authorities say the people who came into contact with the woman are under medical observation, with no signs of illness and negative laboratory tests.You use AI every day. articles.title: DR Congo boat collision kills at least 30, dozens missing
articles.summary: Two vessels crashed while navigating the Congo River in Equateur province at night.
articles.body:
A boat collision on a river in the Democratic Republic of Congo has killed at least 30 people, with dozens more reported missing.

Two vessels crashed into one another as they navigated the Congo river, officials said on Monday. The accident took place on Sunday evening near the Ngombe-Lukolela area in Equateur province in the northwest of the country.

The officials said that 30 people had drowned during the incident. Search-and-rescue efforts have been launched to try to find the missing.

Crispin Mputu, interior minister of Equateur province, told the state-owned news agency Agence Congolaise Presse that “a metal vessel named ‘Dieu se cache,’ was coming from Kinshasa,” the country’s capital, when it crashed with a “wooden vessel called ‘HB Super Victoire,’ [that] was coming from Businga”.

“Almost all the passengers on board were trapped underwater, and the boat itself also sank,” he added.

Mputu said the people who drowned have already been buried.

It is unclear what caused the crash. Mputu noted that many accidents have occurred as boats travel at night.

A security officer who witnessed the incident told The Associated Press news agency that the boat travelling from Kinshasa was overloaded with goods.

Boating tragedies are common in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where late-night travel and overcrowded vessels are often blamed.

Poor safety standards and a lack of infrastructure in remote parts of the country also contribute to boating disasters, which have killed hundreds of people in recent years.

In July, a wooden boat transporting students back from state exams sank, killing at least 20 people in the country’s Kasai province.

articles.title: In 2009, Google's Eric Schmidt and wife Wendy bought a former fisheries ship; by 2022, the vessel offered free research access and had mapped over 1.3 million square kilometres of seafloor
articles.summary: Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt and Wendy Schmidt transformed a former fisheries protection vessel into a philanthropic ocean research platform that, by
articles.body: Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt and Wendy Schmidt transformed a former fisheries protection vessel into a philanthropic ocean research platform that, by 2022, had hosted more than 1,000 scientists and mapped over 1.3 million square kilometres of the ocean floor. According to Schmidt Ocean Institute, the vessel, named Falkor, was originally built in 1981 as a fishery protection ship. It was acquired by the Schmidts in 2009 when they founded the Schmidt Ocean Institute, an organisation focused on advancing oceanographic research and exploration. After undergoing an extensive two-year refit, Falkor was converted into what the institute described as the world's first year-round philanthropic research vessel made available to scientists at no cost.Eric Schmidt and Wendy Schmidt donated to Italy's National Research CouncilRather than retiring the vessel, Schmidt Ocean Institute donated Falkor to Italy's Consiglio Nazionale delle Ricerche (CNR), the country's largest research organization, comprising 88 institutes nationwide and a marine science community of more than 450 researchers. Under CNR, the ship was renamed Gaia Blu and continues operating in the Mediterranean and beyond.Wendy Schmidt, co-founder of Schmidt Ocean Institute, said that after a decade of remarkable discoveries and scientific research, she and Eric couldn't imagine a better home for Falkor than CNR, expressing confidence that the agency would continue the ship's legacy of ocean exploration, supporting marine science, and bringing the wonders of the ocean to the public.Eric Schmidt echoed that sentiment, pointing to CNR's century of scientific experience and its track record of investing in talented researchers as reasons he believed the organization was an excellent new home for the vessel, adding that he looked forward to seeing what further discoveries would emerge from Falkor's continued work at sea.CNR president Prof. Maria Chiara Carrozza called the donation extremely beneficial for both CNR and the wider Italian scientific community, noting that it would help foster collaboration with international research institutes and universities studying the Mediterranean basin — one of the cradles of human civilization, and a region heavily impacted by human activity. She added that the vessel would give Italian scientists a unique opportunity to pursue multi-year ocean research as part of both European and other international projects.Hosted more than 1,000 scientistsAccording to the institute, Falkor completed 81 research expeditions and hosted 1,056 international scientists during its time in service. The ship travelled a distance equivalent to more than 12 trips around the world while supporting marine research projects across multiple oceans.The vessel's explorations contributed to several notable discoveries, including a 500-metre-tall coral reef in Australia's Great Barrier Reef, deep-sea coral "gardens" off Western Australia, and rare footage of the elusive glass octopus.The mission continues with a bigger shipSchmidt Ocean Institute didn't step back from ocean research after donating Falkor — instead, it transitioned to an even larger vessel, Falkor (too), which launched in early fall 2022 after being outfitted with what the organization described as some of the most sophisticated maritime technology available. At 110 metres, the new ship is significantly larger than its predecessor, and has continued the Institute's core mission: operating the world's only year-round philanthropic research vessel made available to the international scientific community entirely free of cost.You use AI every day. articles.title: American chestnut returns to Bronx Zoo more than 120 years after blight was first documented; 25 hybrid saplings planted on 265-acre grounds; NYC expands 1,000-tree restoration drive after disease killed nearly 4 billion trees
articles.summary: More than 120 years after the American chestnut blight was first documented at the Bronx Zoo, the iconic tree is making a historic return to the same
articles.body: More than 120 years after the American chestnut blight was first documented at the Bronx Zoo, the iconic tree is making a historic return to the same grounds where its devastating decline was first recorded.On Monday, October 5, the Wildlife Conservation Society’s Bronx Zoo and the New York Restoration Project planted the first of 25 hybrid American chestnut saplings at the zoo. According to a release issued by the Wildlife Conservation Society, the trees were donated by NYRP in partnership with The American Chestnut Foundation and will be planted across three locations on the 265-acre zoo grounds.The return marks a significant moment in efforts to restore a species that was once a defining feature of forests across the eastern United States but is now considered functionally extinct in the wild.The blight that changed America's forestsThe American chestnut was once one of the largest and most abundant trees in the forests of the eastern United States. It provided food and habitat for wildlife while also supplying valuable timber for generations of people.That changed at the beginning of the 20th century when chestnut blight began killing trees across the region.In 1904, Bronx Zoo Chief Forester Hermann Merkel observed canker-covered chestnut trunks and became the first person to document the disease. The blight subsequently spread throughout the tree's native range, from Maine to Florida and westward to the Ohio Valley.The Wildlife Conservation Society notes that the disease ultimately devastated the species, with nearly 4 billion American chestnut trees killed over the following decades.Today, the American chestnut survives primarily through isolated trees, breeding programmes and hybrids designed to retain characteristics of the native species while improving resistance to the blight.25 hybrid trees planted at Bronx ZooAccording to information provided by WCS, the 25 new saplings will be distributed among three areas of the Bronx Zoo: just north of the pedestrian path at Tiger Mountain, along the eastern bank of the Bronx River and along the riverwalk.Craig Piper, director of the Bronx Zoo, said the planting is part of an effort to strengthen the forest maintained at the zoo.“This is an effort for us to continue to strengthen the forest that we maintain, and chestnuts would've been a significant part of the Bronx Zoo forest,” Piper said.If the trees establish successfully, the zoo plans to plant more chestnuts in the future.Jason Smith, a director at the New York Restoration Project, also highlighted the tree's cultural and ecological importance. Speaking to Gothamist, Smith said, “Chestnut trees have great cultural significance. This will help preserve our natural heritage.”“People love the nuts. People use the lumber. It has really important ecological significance,” he added.New York's growing chestnut restoration effortThe Bronx Zoo planting is part of a broader effort to bring American chestnuts back to New York City's urban landscape.According to NYRP and WCS, the restoration project began expanding its chestnut planting efforts in 2017, when more than 200 hybrid chestnuts were planted at Highbridge Park in Upper Manhattan, creating what is described as New York City's largest chestnut grove.Nearly a decade later, those trees have grown to more than 40 feet tall and are producing flowers, fruit and nuts.The saplings are hybrids combining the American chestnut with blight-resistant Asian chestnut varieties in an effort to preserve the characteristics of the native tree while increasing its ability to withstand the disease.In 2025, NYRP launched the 1,000 Chestnut Challenge, aimed at expanding the number of chestnut trees across New York City and involving residents in the species' restoration.In the first year of the initiative, NYRP planted more than 80 trees across parks, green spaces and backyards. This year, more than 350 additional saplings were distributed across the city's five boroughs, while the goal for next year is to plant at least 500 more.‘Our urban ecosystem can play a part in conservation’Speaking to Gothamist, Smith said the response from New Yorkers has demonstrated strong interest in helping restore the species.“We've found the interest to be overwhelming of folks wanting to plant the tree in New York City,” he said. “It's really important for people to remember that our urban ecosystem can play a part in conservation.”The restoration effort comes as several native New York tree species, including beech, hemlock and ash, face threats from diseases and invasive species.“Our native forests are really under threat from disease, and so finding the opportunity to bring back a tree that was on the brink of extinction is incredibly important,” Smith said, according to Gothamist.A historic homecomingFor the Bronx Zoo, the new plantings carry particular significance because of its role in documenting the beginning of the chestnut's catastrophic decline.The disease first documented by Merkel in 1904 would eventually transform forests across much of eastern North America. More than a century later, hybrid American chestnuts are being planted at the same institution where that history was first recorded.The planting expands the network of restoration sites across New York while reconnecting the American chestnut with a location that played a unique role in documenting its disappearance.The New York Restoration Project, founded in 1995, has made urban tree planting and ecological restoration a central part of its work across New York City. According to the organisation, it has planted and distributed nearly 300,000 trees and restored more than 300 acres of parkland since its founding.The Bronx Zoo, which opened in 1899, occupies 265 acres of hardwood forest in the Bronx and is the flagship park of the Wildlife Conservation Society's network of urban wildlife parks.The return of the American chestnut to the zoo therefore represents more than a new planting. It is an attempt to restore a species that once helped define the region's forests - at the very place where its fight against extinction was first documented.You use AI every day. articles.title: King's funding for Andrew is not for legal action against police
articles.summary: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking action over search warrants issued ahead of his arrest in February.
articles.body:
Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been told that the allowance given to him by King Charles should not be used to fund his legal action against Thames Valley Police and the Central Criminal Court.

The King uses his own private money to support his brother and to accommodate him on his estate in Sandringham.

But a royal source said that this funding should not be used for a legal challenge being launched by Mountbatten-Windsor against the search warrants issued ahead of his arrest in February.

The former Prince Andrew was arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office in the wake of information that emerged from the Epstein files in the United States.

Mountbatten-Windsor has consistently denied any wrongdoing linked to his association with Epstein.

The former Prince Andrew is not a working royal - so Buckingham Palace no longer speaks on his behalf and is not involved in his legal battle.

But a royal source said the King's financial support for his brother should not be directed towards paying for the judicial review that Mountbatten-Windsor is seeking.

It's not been disclosed how much the King gives to Mountbatten-Windsor, but the funding for his brother was part of the arrangement when the former Prince Andrew was moved from his previous home at Royal Lodge in Windsor.

This allowance for Mountbatten-Windsor is not from the Sovereign Grant, which is the £138m in public funding for the monarchy.

It is drawn from the King's private money, which includes his income from the Duchy of Lancaster, private estates and his own investments and inheritances.

At the time of Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest, the King said the "law must take its course", and the Palace is now distancing itself from the former Duke of York's legal pushback.

Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers are understood to be challenging Thames Valley Police and the Central Criminal Court over the lawfulness of warrants used for searches of Sandringham and Royal Lodge - in what has been Andrew's first public response since his arrest earlier this year.

Thames Valley Police has confirmed it is "engaged in legal proceedings in relation to warrants previously obtained from the Central Criminal Court".

It added: "As these legal proceedings are currently ongoing, it would be inappropriate for us to comment further."

Mountbatten-Windsor, who lost his titles as a prince and Duke of York over his connections to the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, wants a judicial review to consider the legality of the search warrants.

A court hearing on Thursday afternoon will be part of Mountbatten-Windsor's bid to quash the warrants.

The warrants had been issued by a judge at the Central Criminal Court on 18 February - the day before Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested in Sandringham.

"Even if Andrew succeeds in having the search warrants quashed, that would not necessarily be the victory it might first appear," said Nick Vamos, a criminal lawyer at Peters & Peters and former head of special crime at the Crown Prosecution Service.

Vamos said disputes over warrants were not uncommon - but if the police lost on a technical error, they could still sometimes keep what they had obtained in a search.

"The police can apply back to the Crown Court to retain the material if they have grounds to immediately seize it again," said Vamos.

It would need to be a more fundamental issue with the granting of the warrants for the police to be required to return the material from a search, he said.

Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest, carried out on his 66th birthday, followed a series of revelations from the Epstein files, published by the US Department of Justice.

They included emails appearing to show official documents being shared by Mountbatten-Windsor with Epstein and others, at a time when he was the UK's trade envoy.

Mountbatten-Windsor had already been stripped of his titles by King Charles, after emails had shown Mountbatten-Windsor had continued his links with Epstein, beyond when he had publicly said connections had been severed.

After Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest he was taken to Aylsham police station. A photograph captured his departure later that day, looking exhausted, after he was released under investigation.

articles.title: Katie Price ex, Kieran Hayler, told girl not to tell, court hears
articles.summary: Jurors at the trial of Kieran Hayler hear recorded police evidence from the alleged victim in court.
articles.body:
Katie Price's ex-husband, who is accused of raping a 13-year-old girl, told her to "not tell anyone" and said he might "get in trouble for this", a court has heard.

Kieran Hayler, 39, is on trial at Lewes Crown Court accused of three counts of rape and one count of sexual assault of the teenager in West Sussex in 2016, all of which he denies.

Earlier, jurors were told that on the first alleged occasion, Hayler told the 13-year-old he really liked her and began speaking to her about having sex.

He told her it was a "special thing" and they should do it, before he raped her, the court heard.

The court was played the complainant's police interview in which she said Hayler told her how special and "important" the first time was.

She said: "He started crying and saying, 'Maybe I shouldn't take it away from you, it's so important'."

The complainant said she did not have a "conversation" with Hayler afterwards, and recalled thinking "I was probably a bit young".

Hayler allegedly raped the girl again on two further occasions.

The second occasion, she said, was two or three weeks later.

On this occasion she said she remembered waking up to Hayler being there, and after, he acted like "like nothing had happened".

On the third alleged occasion, the court heard Hayler told her she should not tell anyone, and then sexually assaulted her.

She said he told her: "You can't talk about it, you can't tell anyone, I might get in trouble for this."

It is alleged he grabbed her hand and put it down his trousers.

Speaking after this alleged incident, the complainant told police: "I think by that point I knew it wasn't quite right, he kept telling me to 'shh', I had to be secretive and not tell anyone."

She told police: "I tried to forget it for so many years."

In 2021, the complainant contacted the NSPCC charity which referred her to the police, prompting the investigation.

Hayler was first interviewed by police in January 2022 and denied any of the allegations took place and that anything sexual occurred.

He was married to media personality Price at the time of the alleged incidents, before the couple's relationship broke down in 2018 and they divorced in 2021.

Hayler suggested his ex-wife had "launched a campaign" against him when their marriage ended, and the allegations form part of this, the court heard.

The alleged victim is not part of Hayler or Price's extended families.

Price is expected to be a witness in the trial which is expected to last about a week.

articles.title: Footballer Andy Carroll names attacker as TV dance coach
articles.summary: The former England striker tells the Sun he was sexually assaulted by former Fame Academy dance instructor Kevin Adams in 2021.
articles.body:
Former England footballer Andy Carroll has told the Sun newspaper the man who sexually assaulted him in 2021 was TV dance coach Kevin Adams.

The 37-year-old striker first revealed he had been assaulted in his autobiography Owning It, which was published last month. The book did not name his attacker.

Adams, who appeared on the BBC series Fame Academy from 2002, was given a custodial sentence for the assault in 2023, BBC News understands.

He was found guilty following a trial in September of that year and sentenced to 20 months imprisonment the following November at Chelmsford Crown Court.

The newspaper said Carroll had decided to name Adams after becoming aware his attacker's name was in publicly available court documents.

Carroll previously said he was attacked while he was asleep by a friend of his former partner, who had visited his home to watch a boxing match. Carroll was playing for his boyhood club Newcastle United at the time.

He said he was being assaulted when he woke up and threw his attacker out of the house, before knocking him unconscious when he tried to return.

Carroll said in his autobiography that he had "spent a lot of time discussing whether to mention it in this book or not", adding: "I avoided my publisher for so long that they probably suspected I got cold feet."

He wrote: "Scary to talk about but it's made [me] the person I am today as much as any of the good stuff. And if me talking about it helps just one person then good, it will have been worth it."

Adams made several TV appearances as a dancer or dance instructor from the late 1990s onwards.

He has not commented publicly since Carroll named him as the man who attacked him.
